title: James Dyson's Coach House and the 5,127th Prototype
dek: From 1979 James Dyson built bagless vacuum prototypes in his coach house, by his own count 5,127 of them, while debts grew and his wife taught art to keep the family going.

story.event: Building thousands of cyclone vacuum prototypes in a coach house before one worked
story.summary: In 1978 James Dyson saw that a cyclone, rather than a bag, could separate dust from air; in 1979, pushed out of his Ballbarrow company, he set up Dyson Research with one backer, his buyout money and a second mortgage, and spent about five years building prototypes in his coach house, 5,127 by his own count. British and American manufacturers turned the design down; a Japanese licence produced the G-Force in 1986, and the first Dyson-branded cleaner, DC01, followed in 1993.
paragraphs: In 1978 James Dyson, who had designed the Ballbarrow, a wheelbarrow with a ball for a wheel, was annoyed by his vacuum cleaner. Once a thin layer of dust lined the bag, it clogged the paper's pores and the suction fell away. At the Ballbarrow factory he had to build a large cyclone, the kind sawmills use, to pull sprayed epoxy powder out of the air. Building it, he realised dust could be separated by spinning the air instead of straining it. At home he took the bag off his cleaner and connected a cardboard and tape model of the cyclone in its place.

In 1979, after disagreements with his partners pushed him out of the Ballbarrow company, he set up Dyson Research with a single backer, his buyout money and a second mortgage on the family home. In his coach house he began building one cyclone cleaner after another. He had made products before that worked, he said years later, but "I didn't know that I could do it, I just hoped that I could do it."

He kept count. By his own tally, his third child was born by the 15th prototype; by the 2,627th he and his wife, Deirdre, were "really counting our pennies"; by the 3,727th she was giving art lessons for extra money. A 2016 interview added that she grew vegetables and kept chickens to feed the family. Deirdre, a painter, "understood the primeval need to have a project, and that it might take a rather long time," he told Wired. The debts grew, and the house was signed over to the bank. "As you go deeper and deeper into debt, you have to go on," he said.

The prototype he numbers 5,127 worked, in 1983 or 1984 depending on the account. Then came the refusals. Businessmen told him that if a better vacuum cleaner were possible, "Hoover or Electrolux would have invented it", and manufacturers who profited from replacement bags were not interested. In 1986 a Japanese licence produced the G-Force, a pink cleaner that became a hit there. Its income, with a bank loan, paid for DC01, the first machine sold under his own name, in 1993. Within 18 months it was a best seller in Britain.

quote.text: I have not heard of an alchemist being sad. Much gold he reduces to ashes so that he may one day turn copper into gold.
quote.locator: Chapter III, "Concerning Love", Story Illustrative of Patience
quote.source_title: The Bustān of Sadi, tr. A. Hart Edwards, Project Gutenberg eBook #60471
quote.connection: Saadi's alchemist burns through gold, which the translator glosses as a life, hoping one day to make gold, and is never sad. Dyson has called such work stressful but hugely enjoyable. But alchemists never made gold, and this story is told because the 5,127th prototype worked; cheerful persistence cannot say which search you are in.

reflection: Dyson's tally is worth reading for what it records besides prototypes: a child born, money counted, a wife taking on art lessons. A long piece of work is rarely carried by one person, even when only one name ends up on it.

You may be in a stretch like that now, where the attempts pile up and the people near you carry part of the cost. It is fair to keep going. It is also fair, now and then, to tell them plainly what the work is costing and what you hope it becomes, so that the hope is something they share rather than only something they pay for.
invitation: This evening, tell one person close to you roughly which attempt you are on with the work that is taking longest, and ask them what the stretch has been like for them.

cross_checks.claim: By Dyson's own count he built 5,127 prototypes before one worked.
The cyclone idea came in 1978 from an industrial cyclone of the kind used in sawmills.
He financed the work with borrowing against his home and his wife's teaching supported the family.
Established manufacturers turned the design down, in part because replacement bags were profitable.
A Japanese licence produced the G-Force in 1986, and DC01 went on sale under Dyson's name in 1993.

research_notes: The figure of 5,127 prototypes is Dyson's own count, and the story attributes it to him ('by his own tally', 'the prototype he numbers 5,127'). The period it covers varies between his accounts and reports of them: his 2011 Wired column says '5,127 prototypes and 15 years to get it right' (counting to DC01 in 1993); Wired 2012 says five years in the coach house before the 1983 design; HardwareZone (2016) says five years, with number 5,127 working in 1984; Entrepreneur (2025) says five years; Gale's Newsmakers says four years; a 2024 Masters of Scale interview (heard via an unofficial machine transcript, not cited) has him say 5,126 failures over four years; Tes (1997) says 'five thousand prototypes and 15 penniless years'. The story therefore says the working prototype came 'in 1983 or 1984 depending on the account' and does not state a duration of its own. Origin: Tes says he built a sawmill-type cyclone for the Ballbarrow factory, while Wired's 2012 timeline says he saw one at a local sawmill; the story follows Tes and calls it 'the kind sawmills use'. Children: Gale says the home already housed three small children in 1979, but Dyson's own column says his third child was born by the 15th prototype; the story follows Dyson. Wife's work: Gale says she taught school, Dyson's column says art lessons, Wired calls her an artist; the story uses his words. The vegetables and chickens are the HardwareZone writer's account, attributed to 'a 2016 interview'. Debt: Dyson told Entrepreneur he 'eventually' owed over a million dollars, which may include the years up to 1993, so the story gives no figure. His being pushed out of the Ballbarrow company and the single backer rest on Gale's Newsmakers profile alone and are stated briefly. The G-Force income and a bank loan both went into DC01 (Wired 2012; Gale; Dyson on Masters of Scale described a £600,000 bank loan in 1992). Funding is marked bootstrapped: there was one private backer and bank borrowing secured on the house, but no venture or institutional equity. Dyson's own sites (dyson.co.uk, jamesdysonfoundation) and Fast Company's 2007 interview block automated requests and are not cited. The Bustan footnote in this Gutenberg edition glosses 'gold' as life; Saadi's alchemist appears in a story about patience in seeking God, applied here by analogy.
